html:
Native Files and mutation receipts

The Files skill operates on the selected Gateway's filesystem. It offers bounded reads, discovery, metadata and content hashes, text comparisons, exact edits and file management. File contents and paths are data; the adapter does not convert a File call into a shell command. Existing Shell commands remain separate tools. File operations require ordinary capability, permission and resource-scope authorization described in execution and receipts.

Choose an operation

The Files skill also provides file.open_attachment, file.inspect_archive and file.read_archive_member on the Controller. These use authorized context IDs and have separate transfer/archive boundaries described in attachment readers. The Gateway filesystem operations below continue to use paths and their existing revision contracts.

Need Operation and boundary
Inspect a known path file.stat observes metadata and a revision without reading content. A missing path can be a successful exists=false observation.
Read known content file.read returns a bounded text range, tail or base64 byte range. Copy an observed next_cursor exactly for continuation; omit it for a fresh read.
Discover paths file.list lists directory entries; file.find searches names/paths through the Gateway's fd backend. Search options are separate argument tokens.
Search text file.search returns bounded matches and context. Check complete and reason before inferring absence.
Verify bytes or compare text file.hash streams a content digest; file.diff returns a bounded unified text comparison without applying it.
Create or change text file.write defaults to create; replacement and append are explicit modes. file.edit applies exact anchors and file.patch applies exact unified diffs.
Manage paths file.mkdir, file.copy, file.move and file.delete have explicit parent, recursion, overwrite and missing-target options. Inspect their effect receipts.

The argument contracts are the source of accepted fields and limits. They bound serialized arguments to 1 MiB at dispatch, ordinary output budgets to 64 KiB and text mutation/diff inputs to 8 MiB per loaded file. The request timeout defaults to 30 seconds and accepts 1–120 seconds. Helper processes and individual operations impose further bounds. A bounded successful observation can still be incomplete; repeating the same limited request does not establish complete coverage.

Request ownership

flowchart LR Tool[Authorized File invocation] --> Adapter[Controller File adapter] Adapter --> Context[Accepted cwd, revisions and private namespace] Context --> Client[Selected-Gateway client] Client --> Service[Authenticated node-bound Gateway route] Service --> Provider[FileProvider] Provider --> Operation[Path checks, deadline and effect accounting] Operation --> Owner[Read, discovery or mutation owner] Owner --> Receipt[Bounded result and mutation facts] Receipt --> Adapter

The controller adapter prepares accepted artifact aliases, target working directory and task scope. The Gateway client dispatches once through inbound HTTP or the outbound session to /file/operation. It does not retry a mutation or fall back to the controller's filesystem. The service checks the requested node and delegates to FileProvider.

The provider owns an ephemeral cursor generation and a bounded cursor store. It applies configured schema validation, resolves target paths and obtains the Files resource lock for mutations other than dry runs. The Operation helpers carry path policy, deadline, cancellation event when supplied, counters and effect facts. Checks are cooperative; they do not interrupt every blocking filesystem syscall.

Paths and continuations

Relative paths use the call's target working directory. Home paths and artifact-workspace:// aliases are resolved on the Gateway; an alias in one operand does not change another operand's working directory. Environment-variable and wildcard characters in ordinary path operands remain literal. Target Windows paths are kept lexical on the controller, including drive and UNC forms.

FilePaths maps accepted run roots and, when enabled on POSIX, logical /tmp into the run's temporary directory. Parent resolution preserves the logical namespace: /tmp/.. means logical /, not the backing directory's parent. See artifact namespaces for publication and temporary-path ownership.

The path boundary is conditional on accepted scope and runtime policy. An explicit guard permits its root, accepted artifact/temp roots and canonical POSIX /tmp; an observed-root escape follows the configured boundary policy. Task resource paths add their own check. Content opens reject special objects and validate descriptor identity against the initial metadata. POSIX parents are opened without following symlinks; native Windows opens preserve sharing-error identity and avoid following a swapped reparse-point leaf. These checks do not constitute an unconditional operating-system sandbox.

Continuation tokens refer to metadata held in Gateway RAM, with a one-hour expiry, provider generation, namespace and root identity. The store retains at most 2,048 entries and evicts by recent use. Restart, eviction, expiry or changed file identity can make a token stale. A malformed token is an invalid invocation; neither failure silently starts a new read. To observe current content afresh, supply the path and range without a cursor.

Read ranges and discovery coverage

A fresh text read defaults to 200 lines and a 64 KiB UTF-8 output budget. Byte mode defaults to 16 KiB of source bytes, returned as base64 within the output budget. Text is decoded strictly and preserves CRLF/CR/LF separators. Long lines are returned in bounded fragments; partial_line explains a cut before the next line boundary. Tail reads scan backwards in fixed blocks. Neither operation needs a whole-file content buffer.

complete describes the requested observation. An explicit line or byte range can be complete while has_more=true and eof=false; the remaining file is outside that range. An output cap can cut a requested range short. Continuations inherit the prior mode, encoding and chunk sizes unless compatible overrides are supplied. Do not combine a cursor with a fresh start-line, tail or byte offset.

Directory listing is shallow by default, returns at most 500 entries by default and ignores ignore-file rules unless requested. Hidden entries remain excluded unless requested. Its native walker sorts entries, bounds enumeration and reports filesystem errors or exhausted budgets. Search uses the same live walker with ignore handling enabled by default. Pattern compilation is cached, filesystem observations are not.

file.find delegates search semantics to fd and has no substitute search engine when that dependency is unavailable. It permits only search options, limits threads to 1–8 (default four), requests one extra match to detect result truncation and caps the final receipt including diagnostics. Returned paths must belong to selected search roots. Explicit guarded scopes reject --follow, because filtering returned paths cannot stop an external walker from traversing beyond the guard. Cancellation, deadlines and early result limits close the stream and reap its owned process.

Content search defaults to literal, case-sensitive matching, at most 100 matches, 10,000 files and 16 MiB per file. Its portable regex mode is single-line and deadline-bounded. Lines over 64 KiB are skipped with long_line_limit, so their contents cannot establish absence. Match excerpts and context are independently bounded. Binary and special objects are reported in skipped; these domain exclusions can coexist with complete=true and do not establish absence in the excluded content.

Ripgrep acceleration applies only to eligible small UTF-8, BOM-free, case-sensitive literal searches without whole-word matching or CR separators. The helper receives already-read text on stdin with user configuration disabled. Unavailable or unsuitable acceleration uses the native matcher. The returned backend identifies which matcher actually ran; choosing backend=ripgrep does not guarantee every file uses it.

Revisions and safe text changes

A File revision hashes stat identity and metadata, including size, timestamps, mode and native identity fields. It is inexpensive because it does not hash the contents. Use file.hash when a content digest is needed. Supply the observed revision as expected_revision for a later mutation. Copy/move destination preconditions use expected_destination_revision; patch uses a path-keyed expected_revisions map.

The controller can fill absent preconditions from the latest successful File observations among its last 1,000 retained results, restricted to the same run, Gateway, working directory and namespace. Explicit caller revisions win. A copy's resulting revision belongs to the destination. These reused observations do not establish current content or authorize a mutation; the Gateway checks the precondition against the filesystem when it executes.

Single-file mutation helpers preserve detected codec/BOM and uniform line endings. Replacement and append sample an existing file's first 8 KiB for encoding/newline style and warn when the file is larger than that sample. Exact edits load at most 8 MiB, validate each anchor's occurrence count and prepare the complete result before publication. A no-op edit does not replace the file. Dry runs return planned changes without creating parent directories or writing content.

Publication, metadata and failure truth

Create and replacement prepare an exclusive private sibling file. Replacement copies mode/ownership and bounded extended attributes from the still-matching source, then syncs the staged bytes. Publication rechecks the destination revision. New-file publication is no-clobber; existing-file publication replaces the target. POSIX records atomic_replace after successful publication and then syncs the parent directory. Windows reports best_effort atomicity.

The destination changes before the final directory sync. If that sync fails, the receipt must retain executed=true, changed=true and partial-mutation facts. file_synced and file_and_directory_synced describe the achieved durability steps; a returned error does not mean the original content survived. Stage cleanup removes private temporary names and reports residual paths when removal fails. It does not roll back an already published destination.

Append writes directly to the existing file in bounded chunks and records each successful byte count. A later disk-full or cancellation failure can leave a partial append. Parent-directory creation can likewise leave already created directories if a subsequent step fails. Read changed, partial_mutation, bytes_written, changed paths and residual paths together before deciding how to recover.

Extended-attribute preservation uses descriptor-based Darwin libc calls or the available os API. Names are capped at 64 KiB and aggregate values at 8 MiB. Copy failures abort staging; unavailable APIs produce a warning. API availability does not guarantee volume/ACL support. Windows replacement can warn that inherited security metadata may differ. Read-only operations do not scan these attributes.

If transport loses a receipt after dispatch may have occurred, the controller reports possible remote effects and unknown mutation outcome. It does not invent changed=false, replay the operation or claim rollback. Inspect current target state and the last known revision before choosing a recovery action.

Recursive management and multi-file patches

Copy and deletion preflight recursive inventories before changing destinations. This inventory includes hidden and ignored entries and rejects incomplete traversal, including a tree deeper than the supported ceiling. Copying a directory requires explicit recursion. Overwrite supports regular files; directory merging is not provided. Links are copied as links unless supported following is requested, and deleting a link removes the link itself. Each successful change is recorded; the operation does not promise whole-tree rollback.

A same-filesystem move uses native no-clobber rename unless overwrite is explicit. It records both paths before syncing directories. Only a cross-device failure before any mutation selects copy-then-delete: copy all destinations, verify regular file digests and link targets, recheck source revisions, then delete sources. A failure can leave copied destinations and some source entries. Inspect cross_filesystem, destination_verified and mutation facts; multi-entry copying and cross-device moves are not atomic.

Patch accepts exact unified diffs, including /dev/null creates/deletes, with at most 64 distinct targets and a 16 MiB aggregate old/new byte budget. It rejects renames, overlapping hunks, mismatched counts/context and duplicate resolved targets. Parent directories must already exist. A missing final transport delimiter does not remove a target newline; the explicit unified-diff no-newline marker controls that behavior.

All changed outputs and deletion backups are staged before the first commit. Commits then proceed sequentially. On failure, reverse recovery checks that the current file still matches the just-published revision before restoring it, so an outside edit is not blindly overwritten. Recovery temporarily clears the request cancellation event and gives cooperative helpers a ten-second recovery deadline. Read each rollback row and rollback_complete. Even when original content is restored and partial_mutation=false, mutation_occurred, executed and changed can record that writes happened. This is recovery after a non-atomic operation, not a multi-file filesystem transaction.

Implementation and validation

Owner Responsibility
Skill registration Fourteen public tools and the sealed skill description; no native progress stream.
Contracts and resource result schemas Closed arguments, private envelope and optional resource-binding fields, separate from file content.
Common primitives Revisions, cursors, bounded text decoding, pinned opens, staging and effect-preserving receipts.
Windows opens Native handle creation, error identity and ownership transfer to a CRT descriptor.
Diff worker Supplied-data comparison with a 64 KiB returned diff; the parent limits aggregate lines to 20,000 and kills/reaps it on deadline expiry.
Read owner Incremental text/byte ranges, tail offsets, scoped continuations and streamed SHA-256.
Traversal, discovery and content search Live bounded enumeration, portable matching, owned helper processes and explicit coverage limits.
File management and patching Preflight, native rename, verified cross-device moves and guarded patch recovery.

The native File fixtures exercise real temporary files, encoding/newline combinations, revision conflicts, continuation, partial writes and failures before/after publication. The platform fixtures distinguish native Windows/macOS cases from host-independent ABI/error stubs. A skipped native case is an untested platform condition, not a passing result. The integration fixtures cover permissions, selected-Gateway ownership, scoped revisions and lost receipts with local services and scripted model responses. They do not require live inference. The discovery fixtures also check option rejection, process cleanup, output limits and mapped paths. Installer cases use temporary synthetic archives and mocked downloads; they do not install a system dependency or verify a live release download.
